description: We are a driven team of STEM students in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, passionate about space tech, Earth observation, and data science. Our project harmonizes satellite hotspot data (MODIS & VIIRS) for actionable thermal monitoring and wildfire detection. Join us to build an impactful solution in an energetic, collaborative environment! We’re looking for teammates skilled in Python, geospatial data, research, UI/UX, or presentation design to bring this vision to life.
summary:
The project emphasis is on harmonizing historical NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data to produce a more consistent dataset of active-fire activity to be used for fire activity analysis over time.

It is not possible to directly compare and combine raw counts of the hotspots from the two satellite systems due to differences in space resolution, detection sensitivity, and system observation features. We address these differences by validating, harmonizing with statistics, and processing data; we do this while retaining all the metadata and the actual observations.

In it, they have an interactive map with a hot spot mark, a year-by-month fire activity calendar, historical comparisons, statistical analytics, seasonal pattern recognition, and AI-powered anomaly detection. It also strives to predict the future fire activity in regions based on observed records and relevant information.

environmental data.

The main data source is NASA FIRMS accessed with Python-based processing and machine learning, a React-based front-end development, and a NodeJS-based back-end using Express. PostgreSQL/PostGIS is used for spatial data management.

The ultimate goal is to interface many volumes of satellite observations into a platform that is readable and scientifically useful and allows users to visualize fire patterns in the past, detect anomalies and investigate potential future trends.
details:
Our project is an interactive, AI-driven platform that seeks to match up active-fire observations from NASA's two satellite instruments, MODIS and VIIRS, in historical data.

Both instruments can detect thermal anomalies, active fires but with different spatial resolution, detection sensitivity and observation aspects. Thus, such a comparison of raw hotspot counts between the two species is not valid, and cannot be used to directly approximate the total economic health of the fish populations.

We solve historical observations from FIRMS (NASA) and standardize the formats of these observations for comparison, comparing the differences of sensors and apply statistical harmonization methods to generate more comparable measurements of fire activity based on the original observations and metadata.

The platform offers a hotspot map where users can go and see what fires have been detected, and filter the results based on the geographical location, date and satellite the user chooses. It also has a colour coded burning activity calendar for year-to-year and month-to-month exploration of fire activity, historic comparisons between year-to-year and region-to-region and statistical analytics to help in identification of fire activity trends, distributions and historic averages.

It also features tools for detecting anomalies, like the identification of unusual fire activity from AI-driven algorithms, and for evaluating the seasonal cycle, in order to understand that fires may follow a pattern at certain times of year that is not necessarily repeated at others, based on fire stats.In addition, it includes AI-powered fire anomaly detection tools and tools for evaluating the seasonal cycle to capture that fire activity might recur at certain times of year but not at others based on a number of fire stats. Information generated by AI tools can be used for analysis, and AI-generated insights can be summarized or conveyed in a digestible-to-users way, and the data export functionality enables users to download filtered observations and results.

This project has a primary advantage over other projects in its approach to a serious problem that has been encountered with satellite-based fire observation systems: The inconsistency of observations made by various satellite fire measurement instruments. These will enhance the usefulness of the historical fire data for long-term environmental studies, assist the detection of changes in fire activity that are unusual over time, provide seasonal and geographical information to assist with identifying changes in activity, and enable enhanced data driven environmental decision-makers.

We are aiming to increase the availability of large volumes of satellite data to become more accessible and useful to science. The platform is designed to help researchers, students and environmental experts grasp historical fire records and what they might of like to see in the future. Its forecasting abilities are designed not so much for providing a particular location for where ignition of a fire is likely to occur, or when it is likely to occur, but so as to provide an estimate of regional activity and draw attention to those areas that might warrant further investigation.

Data processing, AI and web development technologies are working in unison on the project. The frontend is built with React.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and SCSS, while Leaflet.js is used for interactive mapping and Apache ECharts for graphical representations of data. Backend will be written in NodeJS and ExpressJS and will have PostGIS and Postgresql as databases and geographical data management.

We utilize Python and packages such as Pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyProj, DuckDB, SciPy, Statsmodels, and Scikit-learn for scientific processing and machine learning. We primarily use data from NASA FIRMS which includes historical MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data, and plan to use further environmental data from NASA Earthdata to aid in the analysis.

We also took into account the problems of dealing with large scientific data sets. Given the scale of the historical observations (several gigabytes), we took the approach of using a different storage scheme, host datasets via GitHub for source-code, store data via Google Drive for these to be large and sent to data providers for sharing or processing, and used local data-processing environments and local application testing.

The project's creativity is the ability to achieve more than just placing satellite hotspots on a map. The focus of its innovation is tackling the issue of making observations between two different satellite systems more comparable for long time periods. All detections were not the same and our method takes into account sensor specific features, ensured that the information was not dropped, and created harmonized measurements to ensure a consistent analysis.

We have taken care of scientific correctness, data quality, speed of processing, scalability and accessibility throughout development. We made a brief mention of uncertainty and validation because it cannot on its own be taken as a new fire and the predictive models results can have to be researched carefully.

Our project will focus on innovating the combination of these different technologies, from the processing algorithms for satellite data to the statistical harmonization and combining of the data, on to the integration of Artificial Intelligence, and the development of interactive web technologies, to create a single platform that translates satellite data into meaningful environmental insights.
